title: Assessment Battery Builder
summary: Build a battery for three fictional referrals from seventeen task types, inside a ninety-minute session. The verdict comes in two halves: what your battery could say, and what it could not.
learningObjectives: Select assessment tasks from a referral question rather than from a list of respected tests.
Explain why two measures of the same demand say more than one.
Say why a battery needs a domain the referral does not ask about.
Name the measures that answer no referral question and without which nothing else can be interpreted.
Treat session time as a design constraint rather than an administrative detail.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab. No score is produced for anybody, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native checkbox, select and button controls, each with an accessible name (verified programmatically). Every task label carries its own duration, so the time cost is readable without consulting the chart. The session-time bar is hidden from assistive technology and paired, inside its own figure, with a sentence stating the number of tasks, the minutes used, the budget and whether the battery is deliverable; the end of the session is drawn as a dashed line and named in the axis text. The four checks are a list in which each item writes '(met)' or '(not yet)' into its own text, so the marker is never the only carrier. The control column is a bank of seventeen checkboxes, which is why the primary is pinned - measured at 1366 by 768 the pinned block is 272 to 293px depending on how much is selected and with the submit button scrolled to the bottom of the window the checks are still at the top of the stage. Every selection, preset and submission announces through the shell's polite live region, and focus moves to the builder heading when the prediction unlocks it. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, forced colours are handled, and there is no horizontal page scroll at 320px, 375px, 1366px, 1440px or 1920px.
readmeTopic: Why a battery is chosen from the referral question, and why the measures that answer no question at all are the ones that make the rest interpretable
simulationNotes: Seventeen generically described task types across attention, memory, language, executive, visuospatial and context, with round teaching durations totalling 167 minutes against a 90-minute session budget. The tool evaluates the design of a battery, never a person, on four checks: converging evidence (at least two tasks in the referral's target domains and at least one in each of them); a comparison domain (at least one task in a domain the referral does not ask about); the two context measures that referral names; and total time within the budget. Two softer signals sit alongside: a burden warning above 70 minutes, and a redundancy note when two selected tasks share a narrow measure outside the target domains. One dependency is modelled - recognition of a word list cannot be administered without the learning task that produced it - and a task with an unmet dependency counts towards nothing. The three referrals target language (context: premorbid estimate and sensory screen), memory with attention (context: mood and effort), and visuospatial with memory (context: sensory screen and mood); each has a worked battery of 50, 58 and 65 minutes respectively that meets all four checks. Deliberate simplifications: task descriptions are generic and no published test, subtest, item, stimulus, norm or administration time is reproduced; four checks is a caricature of a real selection, which also weighs language, literacy, education, cultural background, sensory and motor limitations, whether appropriate norms exist and what the person wants from the assessment; assessment is not a task list, and history, interview, informant report, observation and formulation appear nowhere; and the domains are a convenience because every task loads on several. No anatomy, no diagnosis, no prognosis.
